physicalCause: Ongoing continental collision between the Indian Plate and Eurasian Plate (~4–5 cm/yr), accumulating high strain energy along the Main Central Thrust (MCT), Main Boundary Thrust (MBT), and Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT).

seismicZones.regions: Entire Northeast India, parts of Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rann of Kutch (Gujarat), North Bihar (Darbhanga), Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Delhi-NCR, remaining Himalayan foothills, northern Punjab, Haryana, UP, parts of Gujarat, Sikkim, Maharashtra (Koyna region).
Most of the Gangetic plain, Western Ghats, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai, Lakshadweep.
Stable Peninsular shield (parts of Rajasthan, MP, Karnataka, Odisha).

landmarkEvents: 1950 Assam (M8.6), 1993 Latur (M6.2 — intraplate shield quake), 2001 Bhuj (M7.7), 2004 Indian Ocean / Sumatra-Andaman (M9.1), 2005 Kashmir (M7.6).
mitigation: Strict enforcement of Bureau of Indian Standards seismic codes (IS 1893:2016); National Building Code; retrofitting lifelines; NDMA guidelines on seismic risk reduction.

vulnerabilityShare: ~40 million hectares (12% of total geographical area)
physicalCause: High-intensity monsoon rainfall concentrated over 3–4 months; heavy siltation reducing riverbed discharge capacity; drainage congestion in flat plains; river meandering and avulsion.
hotspots: Brahmaputra and Barak Basins (Assam Valley: annual flooding inundating up to 40% of Kaziranga NP)
North Bihar Plains (Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Kamla-Balan, Burhi Gandak)
Ganga Basin (Eastern UP, Bihar, Murshidabad & Malda in West Bengal)
Mahanadi, Brahmani, and Baitarani Delta in coastal Odisha
Tapi and Narmada lower reaches in Gujarat (Surat floods)
landmarkEvents: 1978 & 1998 Ganga basin floods; 2008 Kosi embankment breach; 2018 Kerala mega flood; August 2025 Punjab Sutlej-Beas inundation.
mitigation: Central Water Commission (CWC) telemetry flood forecasting network (over 330 stations); construction of multi-purpose reservoirs (Hirakud, DVC); wetland restoration and afforestation in upper catchments.

physicalCause: High-intensity localized cloudburst rainfall exceeding municipal stormwater drainage capacity (often engineered for only 12–20 mm/hr); loss of natural lakes, tanks, and flood retention basins due to real estate encroachment; paved impermeable surfaces preventing infiltration.
hotspots: Mumbai (Mithi River encroachment, July 2005 944 mm in 24h)
Chennai (Adyar & Cooum rivers, Chembarambakkam reservoir release, 2015 & 2023 Cyclone Michaung)
Bengaluru (loss of interconnected tank cascades / Kere systems, 2022)
Hyderabad (Musi river floodplain constriction)
Delhi (Yamuna floodplain encroachment, July 2023 highest recorded water level 208.66 m)
mitigation: National Urban Flooding Guidelines (NDMA); implementation of Sponge City concepts; reclaiming natural stormwater channels (Rajakaluves in Bengaluru); porous pavements; strict enforcement of National Green Tribunal (NGT) buffer zones around water bodies.

vulnerabilityShare: 7,516 km coastline (especially east coast: 8% of geographical area)
physicalCause: Warm sea surface temperatures (>26.5°C), low vertical wind shear, and Coriolis force over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea during pre-monsoon (April-May) and post-monsoon (October-December) seasons.
basinComparison: Bay of Bengal generates 4 times more cyclones than the Arabian Sea due to higher sea temperatures, enclosed basin geometry, and lower salinity. However, Arabian Sea cyclone frequency and intensity have shown a rising trend in recent decades due to rapid warming.
hotspots: Coastal Odisha (Kendrapada, Jagatsinghpur, Balasore)
Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Krishna, Visakhapatnam)
West Bengal (Sundarbans / South 24 Parganas)
Tamil Nadu (Nagapattinam, Cuddalore)
Gujarat (Kutch, Saurashtra on west coast)
landmarkEvents: 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone (05B, 260 km/h winds, ~10,000 casualties); 2013 Phailin; 2014 Hudhud; 2019 Fani; 2020 Amphan; 2021 Tauktae; 2023 Biparjoy.
mitigation: National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) with multi-purpose cyclone shelters; IMD Doppler Weather Radar (DWR) coastal network; coastal mangrove bio-shields; early warning dissemination via Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) and Sachet app.

vulnerabilityShare: 12.6% of Indian landmass (~0.42 million sq km)
physicalCause: Steep topographic gradients, geologically young and seismically shattered rock strata in the Himalayas; heavy monsoon rainfall saturating slope debris, increasing pore water pressure and inducing shear failure.
anthropogenicTriggers: Unplanned hill road excavation, toe cutting, slope deforestation, blasting for hydropower tunnels, and overloading slopes with multi-storey concrete hotels.
hotspots: Himalayan states: Uttarakhand (Rudraprayag, Chamoli, Pithoragarh), Himachal Pradesh (Shimla, Kinnaur, Kullu), Darjeeling-Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh
Western Ghats: Wayanad and Idukki (Kerala, July 2024 Wayanad disaster ~400+ casualties), Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu), Mahabaleshwar (Maharashtra)
mitigation: Geological Survey of India (GSI) National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping (NLSM); slope bio-engineering using deep-rooted vetiver grass; wire-mesh netting and retaining walls; early warning rainfall-threshold monitoring.

physicalCause: Accelerated retreat of Himalayan glaciers due to climate warming leaves behind massive terminal and lateral moraine-dammed glacial lakes. Loose moraines can breach suddenly due to ice/rock avalanches, seismic tremors, or intense precipitation, releasing millions of cubic meters of water downstream in minutes.
hotspots: Sikkim: South Lhonak Lake (breached 4 October 2023, destroying Chungthang / Teesta-III dam)
Uttarakhand: Chorabari Lake (Kedarnath disaster 2013), Rishiganga / Chamoli disaster (February 2021)
Himachal Pradesh & Ladakh glaciated valleys
mitigation: ISRO/NRSC satellite monitoring of over 28,000 glacial lakes across the Himalayas; automated early warning sirens; controlled siphoning and lowering of lake water levels; restricting downstream hydroelectric dam construction in high-risk zones.

vulnerabilityShare: 68% of cultivable area prone to drought in varying degrees
physicalCause: Prolonged deficit or failure of the Southwest Monsoon, exacerbated by El Niño events, high evapotranspiration, and absence of perennial river flows.
hotspots: Marathwada and Vidarbha (Maharashtra)
Rayalaseema (Andhra Pradesh)
North Interior Karnataka
Bundelkhand (UP and MP)
Western Rajasthan (Thar Desert)
Kalahandi-Balangir-Koraput (KBK belt in Odisha)
mitigation: Integrated watershed management (PMKSY); micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler); promotion of drought-tolerant millets (Shree Anna); farm ponds (Amrit Sarovars); Mahatma Gandhi NREGA water conservation assets.

vulnerabilityShare: Northern Plains, Central India, Coastal Andhra & Odisha
physicalCause: Absence of pre-monsoon cloud cover, dry anticyclonic subsidence, and advection of hot dry air from the Thar Desert and Balochistan between April and June.
thresholds: IMD declares Heat Wave when maximum temperature reaches >=40°C in plains, >=37°C in coastal areas, and >=30°C in hills; or departure from normal is >=4.5°C.
mitigation: Heat Action Plans (HAPs) pioneered by Ahmedabad (2013) and scaled nationwide by NDMA; cool roofs program; adjustment of outdoor work timings for MGNREGA and construction workers; public drinking water kiosks.
